rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh's denial repeats an old pattern: earlier rejecters denied messengers, but God routed them and made His messengers triumphant; the same outcome awaits now.
rows.anchor: miscreants have always denied messengers, but God routed them and made His Messengers triumphant.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This world is a trial: truth's adherents must be tested, while evil's adherents receive temporary respite to act freely and lose any excuse.
rows.anchor: this world is a place of trial. Hence the adherents to the truth shall necessarily be put through trial.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All prophets bring one religion and the same truth, but later followers divide it into factions; the Prophet is told to let them enjoy themselves temporarily.
rows.anchor: All prophets are given the same religion by God and call people to the same truth; however, their followers split this religion into bits and pieces

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents mistake wealth and children for increased favor, though these blessings will precipitate their doom; faithful, humble, sincere, generous believers truly increase their blessings and earn a rich reward.
rows.anchor: the blessings they enjoy in the form of wealth and children are an enhancement of favour to them. In fact, this is going to precipitate their doom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Demanded punishment samples would not benefit rejecters: calamities affecting others teach them nothing, and relief from their own calamity returns them to evil.
rows.anchor: if even a sample of this punishment is shown to them, it will not be of any benefit to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using their ears, eyes, and hearts would make resurrection, recompense, and punishment evident; rejecters contradict their established beliefs to satisfy desires.
rows.anchor: if they use these God-gifted faculties, they will think that resurrection and reward and punishment in the hereafter are obvious realities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the conclusion, the Prophet is to overlook his opponents and seek God's refuge from imminent torment; the rejecters will regret too late that they cannot return to do good.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is asked to ignore the attitude of his opponents for a while and seek God’s refuge from the imminent torment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only people with heavy scales will succeed; God's servants who invite the rejecters to religion will triumph despite being mocked.
rows.anchor: Only they will succeed at that time whose scales are heavy and only those servants of God will triumph

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecters think worldly life is long and deny accountability or return to God, but the Hereafter will make its brevity clear and expose the inability of their deities and intercessors to help.
rows.anchor: Today they think that the life of this world has a long span but in the hereafter they will realize that it passed in a few seconds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The foremost referent of believers is the brave Meccan emigrants preparing for jihad; past-tense success expresses certainty, principally the Hereafter, while also subsuming the promised establishment of God's religion in Arabia and other gains under Paradise.
rows.anchor: The glad tidings of success sounded in this verse relate to the future but they are expressed in the past tense.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khushūʿ means humility and meekness, not merely comfort; Qur'anic uses about lowered voices and submissive hearts show its essence as full inward submission expressed in posture, recitation, and prostration.
rows.anchor: The word ﺧﺸﻮعۡmeans “humility and meekness.” It has been used in the Qur’ ān in different forms.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous sūrah stressed diligence in the prayer's outward form; this sūrah highlights its inner essence as an attribute of the believers promised success.
rows.anchor: This signifies diligence in the outer form of the prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laghw includes every activity that distracts from seeking God's pleasure, whether formally prohibited or not; humble prayer makes believers avoid useless conduct and, consequently, sin and vulgarity.
rows.anchor: The word ﻐۡﻮﻟَ refers to every act that can make a person indifferent to the real purpose of life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer rebukes believers and reminds them five times daily of God's pleasure, their destiny, and the preparations and strategy required for it, as stated in 29:45.
rows.anchor: It means that the prayer effectively rebukes him and reminds him five times a day the deeds he is required to do to please God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording also sarcastically targets opponents' frivolous anti-Islam activities, a secondary meaning signaled by the following verse.
rows.anchor: it is also a sarcastic remark on the frivolous activities the opponents were continuously engaging in against Islam and the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parallel passages say God's servants ignore nonsensical talk and pass frivolity with dignity; here they are busy remembering God and reflecting on revelation rather than opponents' chatter.
rows.anchor: In the light of these parallel verses, the verse under discussion also implies that God’s servants spend their time in remembering their Lord and in reflection on His revelations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakāh is the second pillar and, though its legal form varied across religions, broadly means spending for God's cause; in this Makkan sūrah it means charity, not purification as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: here it is not used as term; it refers to charity in general. Those have interpreted it in the connotation of a verbal noun to mean “purification” are mistaken.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer joins a person to God and zakāh to fellow people; together they make one rightly connected to Creator and community worthy of success in both worlds.
rows.anchor: The prayer joins a person with God and zakāh joins him to his brethren.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer and zakāh are two arms of faith grounded in gratitude: gratitude moves believers to pray, spend, and sacrifice, so zakāh manifests and complements prayer and each necessitates the other.
rows.anchor: the common thing between both is gratitude to God. It is this sense of gratitude that urges a believer to the prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier point about humble, fearful prayer preventing sin leads into the additional benefits of prayer discussed next.
rows.anchor: the essence of the prayer is also humility and fear, as mentioned earlier. In this capacity, it stops a person from every sin and vulgarity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sexual desire may be satisfied with wives or slave-maidens within God's limits; transgressors breach those limits, while permitted satisfaction should not be condemned as irreligious, as ascetic ideologies do.
rows.anchor: The verse states that satisfying the sexual urge within limits is allowed; none can be blamed if they remain in these limits.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse names transgressors' crime but omits its punishment to express severe anger and aversion, since silence can be more eloquent.
rows.anchor: Here only their crime is mentioned; its punishment is not. The reason is to express severe anger and aversion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author contrasts the Qur'anic limits with contemporary Western-influenced societies, where he says only coercion is restricted and otherwise sexual freedom is unrestricted.
rows.anchor: the only restriction in this matter relates to coercion and compulsion. If this is not the case, then every person has every type of freedom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trusts include God-given capacities, duties, blessings, entrusted property, and social responsibilities; covenants include those grounded in human nature or revelation and every explicit or customary promise to God or people.
rows.anchor: ﻣٰﻨٰﺖ  refers to all trusts which our Lord has blessed us with in the form of strengths, abilities, obligations and responsibilities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers described are faithful to God and other people, neither rebelling against the Lord nor betraying creatures or breaking their word.
rows.anchor: They are neither dishonest and rebellious in the matter of their Lord nor are ones who are unfaithful to His creatures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trust-and-promise verse comprehensively gathers religious, moral, legal, and social duties revered by every sharīʿah; its details are distributed throughout the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: Here it is a comprehensive statement made after the earlier directives and is in fact a detail of what is concise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer protects all covenants because it is itself a covenant with the Lord, renewed five times daily, and recalls the believer's other promises and responsibilities.
rows.anchor: The prayer itself, as is evident from the explanation of S ūrah al-Baqarah, is a person’s covenant with his Lord.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage begins and ends with prayer: first its humility, then its punctual guarding; its blessings require both, like a Paradise plant needing diligent nourishment.
rows.anchor: this section of verses began with the mention of the prayer and ends on it too.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer safeguards the whole religion by developing and protecting virtue; abandoning it impedes good deeds and causes religion's moral structure to collapse.
rows.anchor: it is through the prayer that all virtues develop and grow and it is the prayer that shields them under its safekeeping.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inheritors will dwell forever in the Paradise Adam lost, without fear of expulsion, after defeating Satan; Firdaws is among Paradise's most majestic parts for those who endangered themselves for truth.
rows.anchor: These people will forever abide in the Paradise lost by their forefather, Adam (sws). They will have no fear of being expelled from there.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idolaters did not think idols could save them; they treated angels as God's daughters and hoped pleasing them would please God. The challenge asks them to name any authority recognized even in their own mythology.
rows.anchor: they never thought that these idols have such

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Polytheists' own acknowledgments contradict their beliefs, making the Qur'an truth and them liars; competing gods would divide creation and conflict, whereas one creator keeps the universe intact.
rows.anchor: What they believe in contradicts their acknowledgements. For this reason, what God has presented in this Qur’ ān is the absolute truth and they are absolute liars

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section promises the Prophet near divine help and victory, believers' success, and enemies' humiliation in both worlds, while telling him to overlook their pranks until their fate arrives.
rows.anchor: the time of God’s help and triumph over his enemies is near. The believers will succeed and the Prophet’s enemies will face humiliation both in this world and in the next.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecters will discover that the respite they thought long passed in a blink; they will then deeply regret their conduct.
rows.anchor: audacious to play their pranks, has passed in the blink of an eye.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Quraysh demanded the threatened punishment as proof, the Qur'an answered that challenge in several places, including 10:46 and 13:40.
rows.anchor: When the Quraysh would be threatened of the punishment that visits a nation that denies its messenger, they would ask the Prophet (sws) to bring it if he was truthful.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other passages affirm punishment but leave open whether it would occur during the Prophet's life; here the author reads the threat as foretelling near victory in his lifetime and his enemies' destruction, confirmed by history and 17:81.
rows.anchor: the time of conquest and dominance for him and his followers is very near. It will come within his life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the bleak circumstances of persecution and forced migration, the assurance emphasizes that circumstances cannot thwart God's intent and reassures the Prophet of the promised victory.
rows.anchor: circumstances can never impede God’s intent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer does more than acknowledge the intensity of punishment: it hints at migration as the route of protection, already arranged by God if the torment comes during the Prophet's life.
rows.anchor: It also insinuates migration requesting God to open this way for them in case this torment was due to come in his own life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should patiently forgive and overlook his opponents, respond magnanimously, leave their mischief to God, and not grieve because judgment is near.
rows.anchor: He should continue to respond to their ill-ways in a magnanimous way. He should not be sad at their taunts and harassment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer seeks patience and strength to forgive enemies; devils include jinn who whisper evil suggestions and human beings displaying the opponents' behavior.
rows.anchor: refer to devils both the jinn who whisper evil suggestions in the heart of people and also those among human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents persist in mischief until death, then awaken to the next world; their plea to return is futile because the time for action ended at death and a barrier lasts until resurrection.
rows.anchor: The time of action for them will stand expired for it is restricted to the previous world only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative reading takes the words to mean that the speaker may utter this plea but would repeat his former conduct if returned.
rows.anchor: can also mean that this person may utter these words but if he is sent back, he will continue to do what he did earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although parallel Qur'anic passages support the alternative, the author prefers the reading that the plea is regret which cannot avail the dead.
rows.anchor: However, in my opinion, the interpretation I have adopted is the correct one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the trumpet, family and tribal bonds will not help, and people will have no time even to seek help from one another; such aid was especially important among Arabs.
rows.anchor: The biggest support a person can have in this world at time of adversity is his family and tribe. For the Arabs, this support had a special significance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here tasaʾul means seeking mutual help from one another.
rows.anchor: here means “to seek mutual help from one another.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only deeds will matter on Judgment Day; relationships will not avail anyone.
rows.anchor: On that day, only deeds – and not relationships – will be any avail.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage first gives God's response to the damned, then their confession and plea for release.
rows.anchor: The first of these verses expresses the response of God when these people would wail and cry. Thereafter their confession and request are cited.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khasāʾ means dismissing someone disgracefully from one's presence.
rows.anchor: The word ﺧَﺴَﺄ expresses disgracefully dismissing someone from one’s presence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rewarded servants were especially poor Muslims, whom arrogant Quraysh persecuted and mocked for their poverty, helplessness, and prayers for mercy.
rows.anchor: The word “group” in “a group among My servants” indicates that here specially the poor Muslims are being referred to.
